edges.justification: Book-to-market ratio, measured at the start of the year, reflects the firm’s valuation and influences the stock’s subsequent performance over the following twelve months.
Earnings surprise, calculated during the year, signals the firm’s earnings performance relative to expectations and shapes investor expectations, thereby driving the stock’s return for that period.
The firm’s twelve‑month return informs institutional investors’ buy‑sell decisions, leading to a change in institutional ownership over the following twelve months.
Leverage level, measured at the start of the year, constrains the firm’s ability to generate growth and thus impacts its realized return for that year.
The aggregate market return over the same twelve‑month window affects the firm’s return through market‑wide systematic risk factors.
Historical performance over the five years before the current year carries over into the current period and can influence the current return.
Annual return is a profitability component of the quality score calculated at the end of the year.
Assignment to a value index at the start of the year is based on valuation metrics that influence expected performance, thereby affecting the subsequent return.
A firm’s valuation at the start of the year shapes institutional investors’ perception and influences ownership changes over the following twelve months.
Historical performance affects the market value of equity at the start of the year, thereby influencing the book‑to‑market ratio.
Value index membership is determined by the book‑to‑market ratio calculated at the start of the year.
The month in which a firm’s fiscal year ends determines the timing of earnings reports and thus influences the calculation of earnings surprise.
An earnings surprise provides new information that can alter institutional investors’ positions, leading to a change in ownership.
Earnings performance is a key component of the quality score; a surprise relative to forecasts directly impacts the score.
The measurement period for ownership change begins immediately after the fiscal year ends, making the end month a driver of the subsequent ownership shift.
Quality score is evaluated at the end of the fiscal year, so the month of fiscal year end determines the timing of that evaluation.
Leverage levels affect institutional investors’ risk appetite and therefore influence their ownership decisions.
Institutional investors respond to overall market performance, which drives their buy‑sell activity and changes in ownership.
Historical performance informs institutional investors’ confidence, affecting their future ownership positions.
A higher quality score signals lower risk and higher profitability, attracting institutional ownership.
Being a member of a value index influences the investment flow of institutional investors, leading to ownership changes.
Low leverage is a safety component of the quality score, so leverage directly influences the score.
The market return component of the quality score reflects the firm’s exposure to systematic risk, thus the market return directly informs the score.
Past performance is used to assess historical profitability and growth, key inputs to the quality score.
Historical performance can influence the firm’s valuation and thereby affect its assignment to a value index.
